770754.title: Help for a capacitive wave height sensor

answers.body:
You have not included any construction details and those have perhaps the most bearing on your project.

I have built such a sensor some time ago, and it was rather simple - a vertical coaxial capacitor with a part of it immersed in water. The outer conductor was a stainless steel tube, with plastic coating applied that made for an insulator. IIRC, that plastic coating was rather expensive.

The inner conductor was the shield of a teflon-sheathed coax cable, with the center conductor unused (connected to the shield). Water would flow into and out of this coaxial assembly, changing the permittivity of the space between the coax cable shield and the stainless steel tube between that of air and water - a factor of ≈80.

The coax cable was under tension and was fixed in the center of the tube with using two machined teflon end caps. The caps were split into two pieces that could be pressed together. The coax passes through one cap piece, then has its shield and inner conductor soldered to a washer, to provide mechanical anchor, and then another cap piece goes on it. The immersed 2nd cap piece was blind (no holes). The above-water 2nd cap piece was attached to a box containing the signal conditioning electronics.

The measurement technique was wideband impedance measurement. The output was a list of frequencies, with complex impedance measured at each frequency. From this it was easy to derive both the height of the water column above the bottom of the tube, and the salinity. From what I recall, the performance was quite respectable. The electronics box was hermetic, i.e. gas tight, and was initially purged with dry nitrogen.

The prototype used regular copper coax. For the production run, we ordered a 1000ft of custom coax, with the braid made of slightly thicker stainless steel wire, and the center wire replaced with steel cable. It took tensioning and thermal cycling well.

Today I'd have probably simplified it quite a bit by using a more complex rigid coaxial tube assembly. Going from outside in: plastic, stainless, plastic, measurement gap, plastic, stainless. That could be put together rather easily from off-the-shelf tube stock.

question_comments.body: @AmitM You need to sort-out the actual question you want to ask because without that being clear and unambiguous, you don't have a proper post. You should also not embed a question that refers to \$V_1\$ and \$I_2\$ then expect people to want to follow your reasoning when you rename those quantities. Also, where is figure 5.32? What is the use of your first image? Why does it use k as the turns ratio when k is also referred to as the duty cycle?

Why would the input voltage change unless it was a change in the input voltage that naturally causes a 5% change in the duty cycle. In other words, cause and effect seem to be mixed-up in your question. And, if it is the input voltage changing that causes a duty cycle change then that duty change woud be to stabilize the output voltage hence, why should the output current change? Maybe you have transcribed the question incorrectly or maybe you need to take some other path? Additionally, your images don't appear to show \$V_1\$ or \$I_2\$. Very confusing.
Maybe there is a mistake in the question, and the author is asking about the percentage change of V2 (output voltage) and I1 (input current)?
Yes, that seems likely. There is a mistake in the question. The question seem to ask to solve for \$V_2\$ and \$I_1\$.

The 5% increment in duty is the disturbance (or the small signal duty), d'. From the super imposed circuit (steady state + small signal) you will have to separate out its small signal circuit and then obtain vs', and i2'. Then find out the equivalent % in terms of Vs and I2.

\$V_s\$ shouldn't change because of change in duty cycle. I also think that duty cycle change is for correction of output voltage as you surmised. Why would input voltage change because of change of duty cycle? It didn't make any sense. I had added the original question. Please take a look.

The input voltage could change in relationship with the duty ratio if the input is a current source like with a solar panel. But the symbol shows a voltage source so that is a weird question. I can show you how to determine the small-signal dc gain of this boost without resorting to the small-signal model if you wish, quite easy to do.
The problem does use the letter k for duty cycle and then for turns ratio in another diagram for the small signal model in another diagram in a different context.  Figure 5.32 is Figure 1.

answers.body:
Gate driver will simply open and close output transistors shown in simplified schematics (your first picture), nothing more. It is you to provide appropriate voltages which then be switched by transistors and fed to MOSFET gate.

Normally for NMOS you should provide voltage supply for VCC pin (so for LO Vgs drive level is VCC-COM, typically around 12 V) and then bootstrap circuit will "pump up" this exact voltage VCC-COM (12 V) to VS reference and you will get following (VS is 150 V for example):

  • V(COM) = 0 V;
  • V(VCC) = 12 V;
  • V(VCC-COM) = 12 V (as provided by your external circuit connected to VCC pin;
  • V(VS) = 150 V;
  • V(VB) = 162 V (by bootstrap circuitry);
  • V(VB-VS) = 12 V.

You have to provide PWM (not 0%/100%, switching must be continuous) to high and low-side control to make bootstrap circuitry work.

As another approach you can provide external voltage supply to VB and remove bootstrap circuitry - in this case it's up to you to not exceed Vgs limits.

HO and LO are simply hard-limited to VB/VS and VCC/COM rails as driver simply shorts HO/LO to these pins by internal MOSFET and nothing more. If you try to exceed datasheet limits for HO (VS-0.3 or VB+0.3) you will simply let current through internal MOSFET's body diodes and if current is too high these MOSFETs will blow and driver will be damaged from now.

For PMOS this driver will work normally if you connect VB to high-side PMOS source and provide correct voltage (about -12 V referenced to PMOS source) for VS pin. If you want to make bootstrap work for PMOS I doubt it will work (may work with some complex circuitry which I suppose is not feasible).

771912.title: Single phase full bridge sinusoidal PWM inverter - output harmonic voltages

answers.body:
I was able to simplify the equations further using 6.38(a) and 6.38(d) and using \$T_s = \frac {T} { 2(p+1)} \$.

$$t_{m+1} = t_x + (m+1)\frac{T_s}{2} $$ $$t_{m} = t_x + (m)\frac{T_s}{2} $$

$$d_m = t_{m+1} - t_{m} = \frac{T_s}{2} $$

Now, \$T_s = \frac{T}{2(p+1)} \$

The fourier coeffecient \$B_n\$ is,

$$B_n = \sum_{m=1}^{2p} \frac{4V_s}{nπ}sin(\frac{nωT}{4(p+1)})sin( n(α_m +\frac{δ _m}{2} )) $$

This becomes

$$B_n = \sum_{m=1}^{2p} \frac{4V_s}{nπ}sin(\frac{nω}{4f(p+1)})sin( n(α_m +\frac{δ _m}{2} )) $$

$$= \sum_{m=1}^{2p} \frac{4V_s}{nπ}sin(\frac{n*2πf}{4f(p+1)})sin( n(α_m +\frac{δ _m}{2} )) $$

$$B_n = \sum_{m=1}^{2p} \frac{4V_s}{nπ}sin(\frac{2nπ}{4(p+1)})sin( n(α_m +\frac{δ _m}{2} )) $$

This is sufficient to calculate the fourier series which is of the form

$$V_o(t) = \sum_{n=1,3,5..}^{∞} B_n sin(nωt) $$

However, \$α_m\$ contains the term t and is found as

for m = 1,3,5...2p-1

$$α_m = sin^{-1}(( 1- \frac{2t}{T_S} )\frac{1}{M} ) $$

for m = 2,4,6...2p

$$α_m = sin^{-1}((\frac{2t}{T_S} )\frac{1}{M} ) $$

and \$δ_m = ωd_m\$, \${d_m}= \frac{T_s}{2} \$. Therefore,

$$\frac{δ_m}{2}= \frac{ωT_s}{2} =\frac{ωT}{4(p+1)} $$

769368.title: Fuzzy Logic Controller - 120 V silicone heat pad to metal shelf - Question on output for temp delay

answers.body:
Input to the FLC is delta temp error, possibly rate of change of temp error if that should be in the FLC or be used to modify the FLC output (question).

Yes, you could measure the delta temperature rise say every few seconds or so, and use that to reduce the PWM duty-cycle as it gets close to the desired temperature.

1. When picking a period of 3 seconds, there is an assumption that the thermal time constant of your tray heater is >> 3 seconds. I'll presume that is true so that your sample period is much smaller than the time constant of your load. I am assuming the load time constant is what you are referring to as your lag. What are your accuracy, response specs? If the (time constant)/(decision period) ratio is too low, your sampling rate is too low - this needs to be addressed before you consider your control scheme.

  2. FLC is a non-linear rule-based controller. If your system isn't highly non-linear, you might want to re-think your choice of controller. (My FLC experience is my master's thesis, over 25 yr ago, controlling a SIMO power converter, where I was able develop a rule base to improve on cross regulation over a wider range of output conditions than existing solutions could provide.).

question_comments.body: FL is not some method he is "groping towards".  It's a proven technique  that works well in feedback control loops and handles non-linearities and system hysteresis/deadband generally better then PID, which is predicated on the system response being linear.

This is where the wheel has been well and truly already invented. Look up PID controller, there is a wealth of information about it everywhere on the net. Detect the temperature, and have the PID output a PWM signal. Far faster and more accurate than any method you are groping towards.
PID is not appropriate for what I'm doing and the amount of lag involved.  A better alternative would be be a Smith Predictor but I.ve chosen to use fuzzy logic.
map PWM control to temperature ... that is not a fixed relationship

If you really have a huge lag between actuator and sensor response (relative to system dynamics) you might want to put effort into reducing the lag rather than trying to 'fix it in software'. Anyway, your thought of a feedforward nonlinear term and 'some kind' of FL handling of the residual error (via a model predictive approach etc.) should be workable.

PID controllers can handle lag just fine, especially if you're careful about limiting the bandwidth of the derivative term.  A FLC can also handle lag, in a much more opaque way than any linear controller ever will.  Why are you reaching for opaque when linear controllers are used for this sort of thing all the time?
I'm assuming you mean silicone, not silicon.

answers.body:
I suggest a "race condition"/"setup time" violation as a plausible cause -
something that would just not happen this way with synchronous preset/parallel load:
DOWN_LIMT is used to provide preset values.
When PE is asserted via UP_LIMT, timing is uncritical.
When PE is asserted via DOWN_LIMT, the preset inputs return to L when the OR gate's input returns to L - PE turns inactive after the gate's delay:
I guess 35 gets loaded - followed by 00 at the very last moment.

Remedies include choosing a different counter, shortening the PE signal and extending/delaying the preset values.

I think the overall approach promising, and it should be debugged first.
Then there are several simplifications possible.
The one irking me most:
Drop U6 and use a contemporary '74.
In both 0 and 5, segments a, c, d, f are active.
Additionally, 0 has b and e active, 5 g: any standard logic output more recent than HC should be able to sink 24 mA (2× 'LS47 sink spec) within specs.
Next to go are U16&U17:
Counting up, one 2-input AND each will detect 6 and 3 just fine.
To detect "counted below zero", you don't need to know the count is 9: you can use the MSB (8 or 9); of the "hundreds counter" will be enough.

769280.title: On the behavior of synchronous boost converters e.g. TPS61023 when VIn is slightly below VOut

question_comments.body: Minimum 5V load?|| I understand you need to all this together as it is about a complex subject where multiple aspects interact. I personally consider that entirely reasonable. However, odds are that people will probably close this because of the range of questions. If they do, do not be discouraged. Break up into useful smaller parts and try again.

Too brief and ill defined to be an answer: my feeling is that in the area you are dealing with you are in the hands of the designer and design happenstance. Results may even be determined by device spread as you are at parameter boundaries. If it is important to you I suggest that you build say ten devices and see how they behave. It would probably even be wise to try and get different dated chips as far apart as possible. || Understanding the pass through specifications as well as the data sheet allows will (probably) be important.

A boost converter can only boost (see en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boost_converter), so you cannot have an output voltage lower than your input voltage, in your case 5V. If you want to convert to a lower voltage, use a buck converter, or a buck-boost if you need both things.

You're driving many servos, perhaps all having a common ground. A stalling servo pulls a lot of current, which may feed back along the common ground connection causing a problem for the processor. Another possibility is an intermittent feedback pot inside the other gripper, jarred by the bumped/stalled chopper servo. Both of these are hard to debug, but it might be wise to determine whether it is one or the other.
In this context, "latch up" is CMOS latch up, which is cleared by cycling power. You can do a web search on it.
For serious and non-toy projects like this an oscilloscope is a prerequisite.

@TimWescott Oh, then that does fit the symptoms much better! How would I solve that kind of latch-up? I'll get a decent oscilloscope but until it arrives I could try a solution and see if the problem goes away.

Latchups are  often caused by driving the protection diodes on inputs and outputs of CMOS devices so that the diodes are conducting. In CMOS ICs there can be parasitic bipolar transistors present in the IC layout that act as a latching thyristor. The problem is probably power cables to large servos that are too thin, so the ground of the servo jumps suddenly when overloaded , driving its input beyond the supply voltage rails of the PCA9865, at which point current flows. Adding series resistors from the PCA9865 outputs may help protect it and the servos from latching up.
What details or clarifications is my question missing? Why was it closed?

@glen_geek Yes, they do have a common ground. But how would a jolt to the potentiometer cause continuous spinning? And do you know how I could tell them apart? The PCA9685 sends signals to the servos constantly by the way, I will add that to the question in case it's relevant.

View the faulty gripper servo's PWM logic signal with oscilloscope - as close to the servo as you can probe. If the fault disturbs its PWM signal, look to the PCA9685 or processor as the fault source. If the fault causes no change to the gripper's PWM signal, look to the gripper servo itself for a fault. If the faulty gripper's PWM changes, the PCA9685 or processor may have latched-up...powering down & back up resets the latch-up fault. Re-arranging servo ground connections might fix latch-up.
